/.title: A knowledge business after ChatGPT (Stack Overflow)
/.company: Stack Overflow, the question-and-answer site for programmers
/.problem: Can we predict how many questions developers will ask on Stack Overflow in the next three to six months, as AI assistants take over?
/.protocol_line: Every prediction is made from weeks before its cutoff and scored on the 26 weeks after it; the design was frozen on the first quarter of the cutoffs.
/.situation: OpenAI released ChatGPT on 30 November 2022. Within a year developers were asking AI assistants the questions they used to post on Stack Overflow, and weekly new questions fell by more than half.
/.data_used: Weekly counts of new Stack Overflow questions from March 2021 to October 2026, from the public Stack Exchange API (content CC BY-SA; counts exclude deleted questions).
/.intro: Rebuilds Stack Overflow's question flow as a population of would-be askers. Each week every asker who still posts questions may switch to an AI assistant, and some switch back, with hazards that follow a diffusion curve calibrated on the weeks before the cutoff; the questions that reach the site are the pre-ChatGPT trend and seasonality times the askers who have not switched. Predictions are scored against the questions actually posted in the 13 and 26 weeks after each cutoff, and from the launch week itself. The alternative asks how many questions the site would have kept if the switch to AI assistants had gone half as fast.
/.world: Stack Overflow's would-be askers as one population of 1,000 simulated developers who post their questions on the site or ask an AI assistant instead; the question volume without AI comes from the trend and seasonality before the launch.
/.source: manifests/sources.json (Stack Exchange API v2.3, question counts; content CC BY-SA)

evaluation.cutoffs: the launch week (2022-11-28) and 46 Mondays four weeks apart from 2023-01-23 to 2026-07-06
evaluation.horizons: weeks 1-13 and 14-26 after the cutoff; from the launch week also weeks 27-52
evaluation.calibration: at each cutoff, backtests whose targets fall before it; the no-AI baseline from weeks before the launch

scenarios.title: Stack Overflow as it happened: askers switching to AI assistants from the cutoff
scenarios.description: From each cutoff, carry the would-be askers forward for a year: each week askers switch to AI assistants (or come back) with the hazards of the diffusion path calibrated on the weeks before the cutoff, and the questions that reach the site are the pre-launch trend and seasonality times the askers who still post.

scenarios.title: What if askers had switched to AI assistants half as fast from the cutoff?
scenarios.short_title: Switch to AI at half speed
scenarios.summary: Askers who still post switch to AI assistants at half the simulated hazard from the cutoff; same cutoffs and seeds.
scenarios.description: A slower switch (for example, if the site had kept more askers with its own AI answers) halves the weekly probability that an asker who still posts on Stack Overflow moves to an AI assistant. The size of the change is authored, not estimated.

narrative.subtitle: Can we predict how many questions developers will ask on Stack Overflow in the next three to six months, as AI assistants take over?
takeaways: On 35 held-out cutoffs (67 predictions) the simulation's error was 5,718 questions, lower than the best standard method (damped trend, 9,350 questions): 38.8% less error.
Accuracy, 100 x (1 - error / mean actual): 87.2% for the simulation and 79.1% for damped trend.
Over all 47 cutoffs, including the 12 used to design it: 10,405 questions against 14,650 questions (damped trend).
Weeks 1-13 after the cutoff: 3,603 questions for the simulation, 5,417 questions for damped trend; 66% of actual outcomes inside the simulation's 90% range.
Weeks 14-26 after the cutoff: 8,031 questions for the simulation, 13,653 questions for damped trend; 50% of actual outcomes inside the simulation's 90% range.
Weeks 27-52 after the cutoff: 27,351 questions for the simulation, 39,059 questions for linear trend; 42% of actual outcomes inside the simulation's 90% range.

qa.question: How many of your group will be using the technology by the end of the horizon?
qa.answer: At 2026-07-06 about 98.1% of us use it; in the simulation that is 99.7% after 52 periods (+1.6 points).

qa.answer: In the simulation, we follow the others who already use it, in our own group and in the whole population.

properties.description: The company or group being simulated. Root of the org-unit tree.
A division, department or team. Units nest (part_of) and hold people and roles.
An employee, played as a digital twin: real covariates, a fixed trait layer, weekly latent states and a seat whose policy makes its decisions. Archetypes when the data has no individuals.
A job in this organisation (e.g. purchasing clerk, software engineer). Bound to one O*NET-SOC occupation; performs the instance's activities.
An O*NET-SOC 31.0 occupation, the shared vocabulary that lets roles in different companies be compared.
O*NET generalized work activity: the top level of the activity hierarchy (41 items).
O*NET intermediate work activity (332 items), between GWAs and DWAs.
O*NET detailed work activity (2,087 items). Every instance activity maps to at least one DWA.
An O*NET occupation-specific task statement.
Something a role does in this organisation on the simulated clock (an event-log step, a customer call, a code review). Carries a weight and a remote-feasibility flag.

A tool or software system (ERP, CRM, code repository) that exposes capabilities.

A job in this organisation (e.g. purchasing clerk, software engineer). Bound to one O*NET-SOC occupation; performs the instance's activities.
An O*NET-SOC 31.0 occupation, the shared vocabulary that lets roles in different companies be compared.
O*NET generalized work activity: the top level of the activity hierarchy (41 items).
O*NET intermediate work activity (332 items), between GWAs and DWAs.
O*NET detailed work activity (2,087 items). Every instance activity maps to at least one DWA.
An O*NET occupation-specific task statement.
Something a role does in this organisation on the simulated clock (an event-log step, a customer call, a code review). Carries a weight and a remote-feasibility flag.
The unit of work that flows through activities: a purchase-order line, a case, a ticket.
A document or output an activity produces (invoice, merged code change, review).
A tool or software system (ERP, CRM, code repository) that exposes capabilities.
One thing a system can do, in the MCP sense; activities use capabilities. Automating a capability is a policy lever.
A place work happens: an office, a home, a plant. Hybrid-work policies move people between locations.
A vendor, client or customer outside the organisation that interacts with its activities.
A communication between people (email, chat, meeting invitation).
An intervention or scenario lever: a work-from-home offer, an automation, a hiring wave. Affects roles, activities, capabilities, units or locations.
One recorded occurrence on the clock: a person performed an activity on a work item at a time. The trace is a sequence of events.
A latent, time-varying quantity attached to a person: job satisfaction, work-life balance, attachment, commute burden. Updated weekly by the kernel.

properties.description: One per simulated would-be asker: posts on Stack Overflow or asks an AI assistant

activities.label: Post a question on Stack Overflow

systems.label: Stack Overflow question and answer site

external_actors.label: OpenAI and other AI assistant providers

latent_states.label: Whether the asker now takes questions to an AI assistant

/scenarios/baseline.title: Stack Overflow as it happened: askers switching to AI assistants from the cutoff
/scenarios/baseline.description: From each cutoff, carry the would-be askers forward for a year: each week askers switch to AI assistants (or come back) with the hazards of the diffusion path calibrated on the weeks before the cutoff, and the questions that reach the site are the pre-launch trend and seasonality times the askers who still post.

/scenarios/slower_switch.title: What if askers had switched to AI assistants half as fast from the cutoff?
/scenarios/slower_switch.short_title: Switch to AI at half speed
/scenarios/slower_switch.description: A slower switch (for example, if the site had kept more askers with its own AI answers) halves the weekly probability that an asker who still posts on Stack Overflow moves to an AI assistant. The size of the change is authored, not estimated.
/scenarios/slower_switch.summary: Askers who still post switch to AI assistants at half the simulated hazard from the cutoff; same cutoffs and seeds.
